what_its_for: Agalsidase beta is used to treat Fabry disease, a rare inherited condition where your body cannot make enough of an enzyme called alpha-galactosidase A. Without this enzyme, a fatty substance called GL-3 builds up in your blood vessels and organs, causing pain, kidney problems, heart problems, and stroke. This medicine replaces the missing enzyme to help reduce this buildup and protect your organs.
how_to_take: Agalsidase beta is NOT a pill or tablet. It is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion directly into your vein by a healthcare provider. This is usually done in a clinic, infusion center, or hospital. Each infusion takes about 2 hours or longer, depending on your dose. You will be monitored during and after each infusion for any reactions. Do not try to give this medicine to yourself at home unless your doctor has specifically trained you to do so.
dosing: The usual dose is 1 mg per kilogram (kg) of your body weight, given once every 2 weeks. Your doctor will calculate the exact dose that is right for you based on your weight. Never change your dose or infusion schedule without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: Because this medicine is given by a healthcare provider in a clinical setting, it is important to keep all of your scheduled appointments. If you need to cancel or miss an appointment, call your doctor or infusion center as soon as possible to reschedule. Try not to skip infusions, as missing doses may allow the fatty buildup to return and worsen your condition.
storage: Agalsidase beta is stored and handled by healthcare professionals. If you are storing it at home under special instructions, keep the vials refrigerated between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do not freeze it. Once mixed (reconstituted) by a healthcare provider, the solution should be used right away or stored in the refrigerator and used within 24 hours. Keep it away from direct light and out of reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor about ALL medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take before starting agalsidase beta. Avoid taking chloroquine, amiodarone, benoquin (monobenzone), or gentamicin, as these medicines may reduce how well agalsidase beta works. Do not skip your infusion appointments. If you feel unwell or have a fever on the day of your infusion, call your doctor before going in, as they may need to adjust your care.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room RIGHT AWAY if you experience: chest pain or tightness, difficulty breathing or shortness of breath, throat tightening or swelling of the face, lips, or tongue, severe skin rash or hives, fast or irregular heartbeat, dizziness or fainting, high fever or chills, nausea or vomiting that is severe, or any sudden numbness or weakness. These may be signs of a serious allergic or infusion reaction. Also call your doctor if you notice swelling in your legs or feet, changes in your urine, or worsening pain, as these could indicate organ problems.
when_it_works: Agalsidase beta starts working right away to replace the missing enzyme in your body, but it may take several months before you notice improvements in your symptoms such as reduced pain or better kidney function. Some benefits, like protecting your heart and kidneys from further damage, happen quietly over time without obvious symptoms. It is very important to continue your infusions even if you feel well, because this medicine works best when given regularly and over the long term.
special_populations: Pregnancy and Breastfeeding: If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, talk to your doctor before starting or continuing this medicine. A pregnancy registry exists for women who take agalsidase beta during pregnancy — ask your doctor for details. Children: Agalsidase beta can be used in children as young as 2 years old. Dosing is based on the child's weight. Elderly Patients: There is limited data in patients over 65 years old, but dose adjustments are not routinely required. Your doctor will monitor you closely. Kidney or Liver Problems: Your doctor will monitor your kidney function closely during treatment, as Fabry disease itself affects the kidneys. Patients with Fabry Disease Antibodies: Some patients develop antibodies to this medicine over time, which may reduce its effectiveness. Your doctor may check for antibodies and adjust your care if needed.
